content.title: Integral and p-Series Tests for Convergence
content.overview: This lesson focuses on determining the convergence or divergence of infinite series with positive terms using the p-series criterion and the Integral Test. These methods rely on comparing the behavior of a discrete series to the behavior of a continuous function or a specific power-law form.
learning_objectives: Apply the p-series test to determine convergence based on the exponent p.
Verify the necessary conditions (positive, continuous, decreasing) for the Integral Test.
Evaluate improper integrals to conclude the convergence or divergence of a related series.
Communicate mathematical justifications using proper notation and test criteria.

sections.title: The p-Series Test
sections.content: A p-series is a specific type of infinite series of the form Σ (1 / n^p) for n = 1 to ∞. The convergence of this series depends entirely on the value of the exponent p. If p > 1, the series converges. If 0 < p ≤ 1, the series diverges. A special case is p = 1, known as the harmonic series (Σ 1/n), which always diverges. When applying this test, ensure the series is rewritten in the form n^(-p) to clearly identify the value of p.

sections.title: The Integral Test Requirements
sections.content: The Integral Test relates the convergence of a series Σ a_n to the convergence of an improper integral ∫ f(x) dx. For the test to be valid, the function f(x) where f(n) = a_n must satisfy three conditions on the interval [k, ∞): it must be continuous, positive, and decreasing. To prove a function is decreasing, one typically shows that its derivative f'(x) is less than or equal to zero for all x in the interval.

sections.title: Executing the Integral Test
sections.content:
If the three conditions are met, the series Σ a_n and the improper integral ∫ f(x) dx from k to ∞ behave identically: either both converge or both diverge. To evaluate the improper integral, replace the upper bound with a variable (e.g., 'b'), take the limit as b approaches infinity, and use integration techniques like u-substitution or integration by parts. If the limit results in a finite value, the series converges; if the limit is infinite or does not exist, the series diverges.

![A sequence of steps to apply the Integral Test: Define f(x), Verify conditions, Evaluate improper integral, Match series behavior.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/afc2589f-cadf-4a2b-bd7c-03ad03f5e6b4-1786519411232-526.webp)

worked_examples.question: Determine if the series Σ from n=2 to ∞ of 1 / (n * (ln n)^2) converges or diverges. Justify your answer.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Define the function f(x) = 1 / (x * (ln x)^2). For x ≥ 2, f(x) is continuous and positive. 
Step 2: Verify f(x) is decreasing. Since both x and (ln x)^2 are increasing functions for x ≥ 2, their product in the denominator increases, meaning the reciprocal f(x) decreases. 
Step 3: Set up the improper integral: ∫ from 2 to ∞ of 1 / (x * (ln x)^2) dx. 
Step 4: Use u-substitution. Let u = ln x, then du = (1/x) dx. The bounds change from [2, ∞) to [ln 2, ∞). 
Step 5: Evaluate the integral: ∫ u^(-2) du = [-1/u] from ln 2 to ∞. 
Step 6: Calculate the limit: lim (b→∞) [-1/b - (-1/ln 2)] = 0 + 1/ln 2 = 1/ln 2. 
Step 7: Conclusion: Since the integral converges to a finite value, the series converges by the Integral Test.

common_mistakes: Applying the Integral Test to series with alternating signs (terms must be positive).
Forgetting to check if the function is decreasing before integrating.
Confusing the p-series rule (p > 1 converges) with the Geometric Series rule (|r| < 1 converges).
Assuming the sum of the series is equal to the value of the improper integral (they share behavior, not necessarily the same total value).
exam_tips: Always explicitly state that the function is continuous, positive, and decreasing to earn full justification points.
When p is a decimal (e.g., 1.001), it still follows the p > 1 rule for convergence.
Use the p-series test as a shortcut whenever possible to save time over the Integral Test.
Show the limit notation for improper integrals; writing 'infinity' as a plug-in value is often penalized.
content.recap: The p-series test is a quick tool for series of the form 1/n^p, where p > 1 indicates convergence. For more complex terms, the Integral Test provides a bridge between discrete sums and continuous integration, provided the function is positive, continuous, and decreasing.

knowledge_claims.content: A p-series is defined as the infinite sum of 1/n^p for n = 1 to infinity.
A p-series converges if and only if the exponent p is strictly greater than 1.
A p-series diverges if the exponent p satisfies the condition 0 < p ≤ 1.
The harmonic series is a p-series where p = 1, and it is always divergent.
To use the Integral Test, one must first define a function f(x) such that f(n) matches the terms of the series a_n.
The Integral Test requires the function f(x) to be continuous, positive, and decreasing on the interval of integration.
Decreasing behavior of f(x) can be verified by showing that the first derivative f'(x) is less than or equal to zero on the relevant interval.
If the improper integral of f(x) from k to infinity converges to a finite value, then the corresponding infinite series also converges.
If the improper integral of f(x) from k to infinity diverges, then the corresponding infinite series also diverges.
It is a misconception that the sum of a convergent series is equal to the value of its corresponding improper integral.
The Integral Test is only applicable to series with positive terms; it cannot be used directly for alternating series.
Evaluating an improper integral for the Integral Test requires using limit notation as the upper bound approaches infinity.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Integral and p-Series Tests — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Integral and p-Series Tests: Positive decreasing terms may be compared with an improper integral, and a p-series converges exactly when its exponent exceeds one.
options.B: Algebraic Evaluation of Limits: Direct substitution works when expressions are continuous; indeterminate forms may require factoring, rationalizing, or equivalent algebraic restructuring.
options.C: Chain Rule: The derivative of a composite function multiplies the derivative of the outer function evaluated at the inner function by the inner derivative.
options.D: Local Linearity and L'Hospital's Rule: A differentiable function is locally approximated by its tangent line, while eligible indeterminate quotients may be evaluated by comparing derivatives.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Positive decreasing terms may be compared with an improper integral, and a p-series converges exactly when its exponent exceeds one. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Integral and p-Series Tests — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuity at a point requires an existing limit equal to the function value, and the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees attained values under interval continuity.
options.B: Integral and p-Series Tests: Positive decreasing terms may be compared with an improper integral, and a p-series converges exactly when its exponent exceeds one.
options.C: Implicit Differentiation: When variables are related implicitly, differentiating both sides with respect to the independent variable introduces derivative factors for dependent-variable terms.
options.D: Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems: Theorems guarantee extrema or a derivative equal to an average rate only when their continuity and differentiability hypotheses are satisfied.
